source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: With an oracle label deciding when to stop, self-correction helps. Without it (intrinsic), accuracy falls on every benchmark. Earlier gains came from the oracle, not from the model finding its own errors.
numbers: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 74.7 after 2 rounds; CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 41.8; HotpotQA 26.0 -> 25.0. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 89.0, CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 80.0, HotpotQA 49.0 -> 43.0. With oracle labels: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 -> 84.3, CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 89.7, HotpotQA 26.0 -> 29.0; GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 97.5, CommonSenseQA 82.0 -> 85.5, HotpotQA 49.0 -> 59.0. GPT-3.5 kept its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; when it changed, correct->wrong was more common than wrong->correct.
quote: LLMs cannot properly judge the correctness of their reasoning
limits: Prompted LLMs of 2023 (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Llama-2); temperature criticised later (see b12); HotpotQA only 100 items; reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Direct support for G2: a revision with no external signal is on average harmful. Show the real failing output or do not revise.

source: Tyen et al. (2024) LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error (BIG-Bench Mistake)
finding: Detection is the bottleneck, correction is not. Models fail to locate the first wrong step in their own chain-of-thought, but fix it well once the location is given.
numbers: BIG-Bench Mistake: 2186 CoT traces, 5 tasks, step-level human labels. GPT-4 best, overall mistake-finding accuracy 52.87 with direct step prompting; GPT-3.5-Turbo near floor on some tasks (1.67 to 19.00). Backtracking with oracle location: +18 to +44 points on originally wrong traces, 0 to -11 on originally right traces. With RANDOM location: +5 to +22 gain but -7 to -16 loss.
quote: LLMs cannot find reasoning errors, but can correct them given the error
limits: Tasks are synthetic (word sorting, logic, Dyck, arithmetic, shuffled objects); traces from PaLM 2; 2023 models. Backtracking still helps with a ~60-70% accurate locator.
agent_relevance: Supports G2 and the human finding that detection is the hard step. A code-located failing output replaces the weak detection step. Wrong location is costly: it breaks right answers.

source: Kamoi et al. (2024) When Can LLMs Actually Correct Their Own Mistakes? A Critical Survey
finding: Critical survey of self-correction papers. Many over-state results through weak baselines, oracle labels or unfair prompts. Feedback quality is the bottleneck.
numbers: Three conclusions: (1) no prior work shows successful self-correction with feedback from a prompted LLM on general tasks, except tasks exceptionally suited to it; (2) self-correction works well when reliable external feedback exists; (3) large-scale fine-tuning enables it. Literature up to May 2024.
quote: no prior work demonstrates successful self-correction with feedback from prompted LLMs
limits: Survey, not a new experiment; later work (b12, b13) partly moves the picture for reasoning models.
agent_relevance: Gives the rule for S5: use external, code-checked feedback; treat prompted self-critique as unproven.

source: Kumar et al. (2024) Training Language Models to Self-Correct via Reinforcement Learning (SCoRe)
finding: Training, not prompting, can create intrinsic self-correction. Base models and SFT variants make net-negative or zero corrections; multi-turn RL gives the first clearly positive gain.
numbers: Gemini 1.5 Flash on MATH: base 52.6% first try, 41.4% second try (delta -11.2); STaR delta -14.2; Pair-SFT +1.8; SCoRe delta +4.4 with correct->incorrect changes cut from 15.8% to 1.4% and incorrect->correct raised from 9.5% to 14.5%. HumanEval: SCoRe delta +12.2 vs base +3.0, Self-Refine -1.2.
limits: Needs RL training; one lab, Gemini models; not a scaffold method.
agent_relevance: Shows the failure is a policy problem (the model changes right answers). A scaffold must gate edits, as G2 does, because we cannot retrain.

source: Zhang et al. (2024) Small Language Models Need Strong Verifiers to Self-Correct Reasoning
finding: Small models fine-tuned to critique and refine gain only if the decision of WHEN to refine comes from a strong verifier. A weak self-verifier gives little or misleads the refiner.
numbers: Average gain of 14.6% over the original model on five math and commonsense datasets with a GPT-4-based verifier; with a weak self-trained verifier gains were minor.
limits: Two small models (13B and below); verifier is GPT-4 or oracle labels.
agent_relevance: Same lesson as human error work: who decides there is an error matters more than who fixes it.

source: Stechly, Marquez, Kambhampati (2023) GPT-4 Doesn't Know It's Wrong: iterative prompting on graph colouring
finding: On graph colouring, GPT-4 is no better at verifying than solving. Self-critique loops lower accuracy, and even with a sound external verifier the CONTENT of the feedback hardly matters. Gains come from extra samples.
numbers: 100 instances: no-backprompt baseline 16%; GPT-4 critiquing itself: only 1 of 100 correct; sound verifier backprompting about 40%; binary vs single-error vs full-error feedback not different; plain resampling at n=15 reached about 40%.
quote: the correctness and content of the criticisms seems largely irrelevant
limits: One NP-complete task, one model, one prompt style; an unusually hard case for LLM verification.
agent_relevance: Warning for G2: a real failing output may act mainly as a stop signal plus another sample. Measure revise vs resample at equal calls.

source: Xu et al. (2024) Pride and Prejudice: LLM Amplifies Self-Bias in Self-Refinement
finding: LLMs rate their own outputs above human ratings (self-bias), and repeated self-refine amplifies the bias. Larger models and accurate external feedback reduce it.
numbers: Six LLMs (GPT-4, GPT-3.5, Gemini, Llama2, Mixtral, DeepSeek), three tasks (translation, constrained generation, math). Self-bias present in all; bias and skew rise over iterations; refinement improves fluency while true quality does not.
limits: Read abstract, intro and main findings; scores on non-math tasks are metric-based.
agent_relevance: Explains why model opinion alone must not trigger revision (G2) and why a model should not grade its own revision.

source: Zheng et al. (2025) ProcessBench: Identifying Process Errors in Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Step-level error finding is hard on harder math, and trained process reward models generalise worse than prompted general critics. Reasoning-specialised models are best.
numbers: 3,400 cases, expert-labelled earliest error step. Average F1: o1-mini 87.9, GPT-4o 61.9, QwQ-32B-Preview 71.5. Open PRMs such as Math-Shepherd-PRM-7B score 47.9 (GSM8K), 29.5 (MATH), 24.8 (OlympiadBench).
limits: Math only; weakest models near floor on hard sets.
agent_relevance: Detection quality scales with reasoning training. Do not assume a cheap model can be the error detector.

source: Gou et al. (2024) CRITIC: LLMs can self-correct with tool-interactive critiquing
finding: Tool feedback (search, code interpreter) drives the gains. The model's own critique adds almost nothing, and self-verification is unreliable.
numbers: On open-domain QA, using only the model's own critiques changed F1 by -0.03 and +2.33 with two LLMs, and could fall below the initial output; with tools, F1 improvements over baselines were 5.6 to 12.4.
limits: Tool choices differ by task; ChatGPT and text-davinci-003 era models.
agent_relevance: Direct match with G2: revise from real output of a tool, not from opinion.

source: Madaan et al. (2023) Self-Refine: Iterative Refinement with Self-Feedback
finding: Self-Refine reports large gains on style-like tasks and none on math, where the model cannot tell whether an answer is wrong. With an external signal telling whether the answer is wrong, math gain exceeds 5 points.
numbers: Reported about 20% absolute average improvement over one-step generation across 7 tasks with GPT-3.5 and GPT-4. Math reasoning (GPT-3.5): 64.1 -> 64.1 (no change). Acronym generation +14.8, code readability +13.9.
limits: Soft-criteria tasks favoured; gains on verifiable tasks are small. Huang et al. (b01) say the oracle-free setting is weaker.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: revision helps where error is a matter of degree, not where it is a binary fact.

source: Shinn et al. (2023) Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
finding: Reflection after an external signal (test results, environment failure) lifts agents. It fails when the signal is wrong: false-positive self-written tests make the agent stop early.
numbers: HumanEval Python 0.80 -> 0.91 pass@1 (GPT-4); ALFWorld 130 of 134 tasks solved with ReAct+Reflexion. MBPP Python 0.80 -> 0.77 (worse). False-positive rate of self-written tests 0.01 on HumanEval Python vs 0.16 on MBPP Python.
limits: Signal comes from self-generated tests, so only partly external; 2023 GPT-4.
agent_relevance: The quality of the error signal sets the ceiling. G2 needs the signal to come from code that is itself trusted.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Large language models have intrinsic self-correction ability
finding: A rival view to Huang et al.: intrinsic self-correction works if temperature is zero and the prompt is neutral (not biased toward changing the answer).
numbers: Claim: with fair prompts and zero temperature, accuracy improves on average with statistical significance across four models; biased prompts can decrease accuracy. Some cells still drop (Llama3.1 on one benchmark 78.17 -> 56.85 with a biased prompt).
limits: Gains modest; mixed by benchmark and model; prompt design carries the effect. Not an independent replication of Huang.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition worth testing: neutral wording of S5 (do not ask 'what is wrong' when nothing may be).

source: Self-Correction Bench (2026) the Self-Correction Blind Spot in LLMs
finding: The same error is fixed when attributed to the user but not when attributed to the model itself. The blind spot is activation, not knowledge, and traces to post-training data that lacks error-correction sequences.
numbers: 14 open non-reasoning models: 64.5% average blind spot. Fine-tuning with 5,306 correction traces cut it by 76.0%. Appending 'Wait' cut it by 89.3% with no training. Reasoning models show a small or negative blind spot. On natural errors, only 4.3 to 10.8% of misses are caught when shown externally.
quote: models correct external errors but fail on identical internal ones
limits: Injected errors are artificial; mechanistic work on 7-8B models only.
agent_relevance: Cheap scaffold lever: present earlier output as external text and prompt a re-check ('Wait'). Tests our S5 design. Parallels human 'cannot see own slip' findings.

source: Reason (2000) Human error: models and management, BMJ
finding: Person approach (blame the actor) versus system approach (defences with holes; latent conditions plus active failures). The aim is to build defences, not to fix people.
numbers: Aviation maintenance: about 90% of quality lapses judged blameless. High reliability studies covered about 15 years in carrier flight decks, nuclear plants and air traffic control. No error-rate data for medicine in the paper.
limits: A narrative review; the Swiss cheese claims are conceptual, not tested here.
agent_relevance: Agent version: do not blame one reasoning step; look for the latent condition (prompt, context, missing check) that let the slip through.

source: Perneger (2005) The Swiss cheese model of safety incidents: are there holes in the metaphor?
finding: Readers do not agree on what the parts of the Swiss cheese model mean. The model may be too successful at stressing systems over individual acts.
numbers: N=85 safety-literate respondents; mean 15.3 of 23 'correct' (66.5%) vs 11.5 by chance. Only 30.6% placed active error as a hole; 20.0% read hole as unsafe act. 89.4% chose 'plugging a hole', only 31.8% 'adding a slice'.
limits: Self-selected sample, ad hoc questionnaire, author-coded answers. Shows ambiguity, does not refute the model.
agent_relevance: Reason's model is a metaphor, not a measured law. Use it to design layered checks, not to predict rates.

source: Helmreich (2000) On error management: lessons from aviation, BMJ
finding: Line observation of normal flights finds errors are routine, and crews manage them through threat and error management. Violations and proficiency or decision errors differ in risk.
numbers: More than 3,500 flights observed; on average two threats and two errors per flight. More than half of errors were violations. Crews that violated procedure were 1.4 times as likely to commit other errors. Terrain a threat on 58% of flights, weather 28%.
quote: an average of two threats and two errors observed per flight
limits: Observer-coded (LOSA); no per-error detection rate in the text; aviation not medicine.
agent_relevance: Errors per run are the norm, so the question for the agent is trapping, not zero errors. Log errors with their threat context.

source: Danielmeier & Ullsperger (2011) Post-error adjustments (two new experiments)
finding: People often slow down after an error, but slowing does not reliably make the next answer more accurate. Three accounts compete: cognitive control, orienting to a rare event, motor inhibition.
numbers: Exp 1 (n=19, flanker): post-error slowing 59 ms at 200 ms interval, 11 ms at 750, -9 at 1500, -1 at 3000. Accuracy after errors unchanged. Exp 2 (n=15): slowing 2.8% then 1.5%, test-retest rho 0.54. Slowing and accuracy gain correlated only r=0.25 (p=0.28).
limits: Small samples. Slowing needs short intervals and rare errors; absent when errors frequent or when correction is required.
agent_relevance: Do not assume 'slow down after an error' is the repair. Orienting is not control. Test whether a pause in S5 adds anything over a plain retry.

source: Danielmeier & Ullsperger (2011) Post-error adjustments: discriminating experiments
finding: Experiments that separate the rival accounts: when correct trials were rare, slowing followed correct trials, supporting orienting. Slowing appears only after self-made errors, not false error feedback. Lorazepam removed accuracy gain but left slowing.
numbers: Notebaert et al. (2009): error rarity flips the effect. De Bruijn (2004): lorazepam abolished post-error improvement, slowing intact. Lesions of right inferior frontal sulcus or medial frontal cortex abolished slowing; thalamic lesions abolished both.
limits: Second-hand summary of other studies; slowing only under accuracy emphasis; telling people to correct errors reduces it.
agent_relevance: Moderators are instructions, error rate and interval. A rare-error regime differs from a frequent-error one, as for an agent that rarely fails.

source: Yeung & Summerfield (2012) Metacognition in human decision-making: confidence and error monitoring
finding: Humans detect errors by evidence that keeps accumulating after the response. Error correction and conscious detection can come apart. Confidence is lower on errors even at matched difficulty.
numbers: Flanker tasks with speed pressure: error rates over 20% on incompatible trials. Error negativity within 100 ms; positivity 200 to 400 ms later and tied to explicit awareness. Antisaccade study: people corrected all errors but detected only half. Changes of mind go more often wrong->right than right->wrong.
quote: explicit error detection cannot be a mere consequence of post-decision correction
limits: Lab choice tasks, not complex work; detection models are incomplete by the authors' own account.
agent_relevance: Support for G2 and a design hint: new evidence after the first answer (fresh computation) catches errors; re-reading the same context does not.

source: Norman et al. (2014) The etiology of diagnostic errors: controlled trial of System 1 vs System 2 reasoning
finding: Telling doctors to slow down and be thorough did not raise diagnostic accuracy. Errors were not caused by speed alone.
numbers: 204 second-year residents (96 in 2010 speed, 108 in 2011 reflect), 20 cases. Accuracy 44.5% (speed) vs 45.0% (reflect), n.s. Time 69 s vs 89 s per case. Wrong cases took 17 s longer than right ones.
limits: Abstract only read. Cohorts were different years, not randomised in the same period.
agent_relevance: Plain 'think more carefully' is not a repair. This argues against a generic reflect step and for specific checks.

source: Sherbino et al. (2014) Ineffectiveness of cognitive forcing strategies to reduce biases in diagnostic reasoning
finding: Training in cognitive forcing strategies did not reduce diagnostic errors from search satisficing or availability bias.
numbers: 191 medical students (145 trained, 46 control). Second diagnosis found: 54% vs 48% (p=0.13). Uncommon diagnosis in availability cases: 45% in both groups. False-positive over-search: 64% vs 77% (n.s.).
limits: Abstract only read; novices, one training course, small control group.
agent_relevance: Debiasing instructions fail as general-purpose repairs; failure is the base case to beat.

source: Croskerry, Singhal, Mamede (2013) Cognitive debiasing 2: impediments to and strategies for change
finding: Review of debiasing work. Reports positive results for deliberate reflection, consider-the-opposite, slowing and checklists, but only minor effect for cognitive forcing. No effect sizes given in the review.
numbers: Cited: Mamede 2008 and 2010 (reflection improved difficult-case diagnoses and countered availability bias), Sherbino 2011 (minor effect), Pronovost 2006 and Haynes 2009 (checklists).
limits: Narrative review; its positive list mixes small lab studies and observational studies.
agent_relevance: Candidate repairs with some support: structured reflection on the actual case, and checklists, not general slowing.

source: Haynes et al. (2009) A surgical safety checklist to reduce morbidity and mortality in a global population
finding: Before-after study in 8 hospitals: a 19-item checklist went with fewer deaths and complications.
numbers: 3733 patients before, 3955 after. Death 1.5% -> 0.8% (P=0.003). Complications 11.0% -> 7.0% (P<0.001).
limits: No control group; abstract only read.
agent_relevance: A checklist is an external, code-like check. Effects may be overstated (see next line).

source: Urbach et al. (2014) Introduction of surgical safety checklists in Ontario, Canada
finding: Failed replication at population level. Mandatory checklists in Ontario were not followed by significant drops in mortality or complications.
numbers: 101 hospitals; 109,341 procedures before, 106,370 after. Mortality 0.71% -> 0.65% (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.80 to 1.03, P=0.13). Complications 3.86% -> 3.82% (OR 0.97, P=0.29).
limits: Observational natural experiment, 3-month windows; checklist use quality not measured. Abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Same pattern as LLM self-check: gains shrink when the check is applied by rote. Check use must be real, not ceremonial.

source: Pronovost et al. (2006) An intervention to decrease catheter-related bloodstream infections in the ICU
finding: A five-step evidence-based bundle with a checklist cut infections and the effect lasted 18 months.
numbers: 103 ICUs, 375,757 catheter-days. Median rate per 1000 catheter-days 2.7 -> 0 at 3 months. Incidence-rate ratio 0.62 at 0 to 3 months, 0.34 at 16 to 18 months (up to 66% reduction).
limits: Cohort without control group; includes culture change and feedback; abstract only read.
agent_relevance: Checks that win combine a short fixed list with authority to stop; matches the S5 stop rule.
